newsitem.title: THAILAND: INTERVIEW - Thai property firm to ride out slump.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Thai property firm to ride out slump.

text.p: First Pacific Davies (Thailand) Ltd said on Thursday it hopes to benefit from changes expected in the property sector once it pulls out of its current slump.

Simon Gray, managing director of First Pacific Davies, told Reuters in an interview oversupply and the slowing economy had hurt the Thai property market. But in the long run the downward spiral would prove good for his company, which provides consultancy and management services to the sector.
"The market will be difficult for the next 12 months for sure. But I maintain that while it will be tough for a while, it will be good in the long term," he said.
Thailand's property sector has suffered from the slowdown in the economy, high interest rates and over-supply.
The central bank earlier this year warned financial institutions to be cautious in lending to property developers due to the possible risks involved.
Gray said the prolonged slump in the sector would help get rid of speculators who had taken advantage of the past decade of rapid growth in Thailand and its resulting property boom.
"Speculation in the market in the long term is not good for the market. Now speculators are gone, and people say they are buying for the long term," he said.
"It's weeding out the speculators, it's weeding out the non-professional developers. And in the long term it helps us."
First Pacific Davies had a variety of different businesses in Thailand, Gray said. The agency side, which buys, sells and leases property, is suffering along with the slowdown in the market.
But the management side was booming, Gray said. First Pacific Davies was currently the biggest property manager in Bangkok, managing 35 properties.
Consultancy was another growth area, he said.

"We're offering an international standard. The market is maturing towards that," he said. "People realise they need help, they say before we lay the first brick let's decide what we're going to build and how we're going to do it."

Increased demand for feasibility studies was a sign of maturity in the market, he said. Developers were realising they could not just build and expect projects to be a success as they had done in the past during Thailand's boom years.

First Pacific Davies was targeting 20-25 percent revenue growth in 1997, and planned to expand to areas outside Bangkok in the next six to 12 months, Gray said. He would not elaborate or give figures for 1996 revenues.
First Pacific Davies is 49 percent owned by a unit of Hong Kong's First Pacific Co Ltd and 51 percent held by a private Thai company.
